## FILE: README.md

```
   1  # Certify-the-Checker
   2  
   3  [![examples](https://github.com/ericyunlinchiang/certify-the-checker/actions/workflows/examples.yml/badge.svg)](https://github.com/ericyunlinchiang/certify-the-checker/actions/workflows/examples.yml)
   4  
   5  **A "no issues found" result from a code checker is only true for what was actually checked.** This repo shows that with
   6  six small, runnable C examples. It also gives a short reporting format for writing down what a CLEAN result really covers.
   7  It is for anyone who uses linters, static analyzers or AI code review. No security background needed.
   8  
   9  ## What this shows, and what it does not
  10  
  11  Shows:
  12  - on six small examples written for this repo, three free checkers (clang, gcc -fanalyzer, cppcheck) sometimes say CLEAN when
  13    running the code finds a bug, and sometimes find a bug the tests never reach;
  14  - why "the line ran in my tests" is weaker than "the risky case was tested", measured with coverage.
  15  
  16  Does not show:
  17  - how often this happens in real projects (these are six hand-written teaching examples);
  18  - that any of these tools is bad. Results depend on tool versions and flags, which are listed below.
  19  
  20  ## Results
  21  
  22  Ubuntu 24.04: gcc 13.3.0 (`-Wall -Wextra -fanalyzer`), clang 18.1.3 (`--analyze`), cppcheck 2.13.0 (`--enable=all`).
  23  "Running the code" = AddressSanitizer + UBSan, one run per kind of input. CI re-runs this table on every change and
  24  publishes all raw outputs (the "raw-outputs" artifact of each Actions run).
  25  
  26  | example | clang --analyze | gcc -fanalyzer | cppcheck | running the code (per kind of input) |
  27  |---|---|---|---|---|
  28  | 01-integer-truncation | CLEAN | BUG | CLEAN | normal=CLEAN large=BUG |
  29  | 02-off-by-one | CLEAN | CLEAN | CLEAN | normal=CLEAN boundary=BUG |
  30  | 03-signed-length | CLEAN | CLEAN | CLEAN | normal=CLEAN negative=BUG |
  31  | 04-use-after-free | BUG | BUG | BUG | normal=CLEAN error=CLEAN error-read=BUG |
  32  | 05-untested-error-path | CLEAN | BUG | BUG | normal=CLEAN |
  33  | 06-divide-by-zero | BUG | CLEAN | CLEAN | normal=CLEAN empty=BUG |
  34  
  35  What the table says:
  36  
  37  - **02, 03**: all three checkers say CLEAN, yet the code breaks on one kind of input.
  38  - **05**: the opposite. Two checkers find the bug, but the tests (normal input only) never reach it: the root-cause line
  39    ran 0 times. Running the code is not automatically better.
  40  - **01, 06**: the checkers disagree with each other. 06 is not a memory bug.
  41  - **04**: all three find it; cppcheck also reports a double free on line 12 that never happens at run time.
  42  - In every row, normal input passes. A test suite with only normal inputs would pass too.
  43  
  44  **Tried another checker or an AI reviewer?** Please share the result with the "Checker result" issue template.
  45  
  46  ## FAQ
  47  
  48  ### Does "no issues found" from a static analyzer mean my code is safe?
  49  No. It means the checker found nothing with its rules, flags and version. In this repo, examples 02 and 03 pass clang
  50  --analyze, gcc -fanalyzer and cppcheck with no findings, yet both crash on one kind of input.
  51  
  52  ### Does the clang static analyzer catch off-by-one errors?
  53  Not in example 02 (clang 18.1.3, `--analyze`): a loop written with `<=` instead of `<` writes one element past a 16-byte
  54  stack buffer, and clang reports nothing. gcc -fanalyzer and cppcheck also report nothing. AddressSanitizer catches it on
  55  the boundary input.
  56  
  57  ### Does gcc -fanalyzer catch a buffer overflow caused by integer truncation?
  58  Yes in example 01 (gcc 13.3.0): it flags the heap overflow when a buffer size is computed in 16 bits. clang --analyze and
  59  cppcheck do not.
  60  
  61  ### Does cppcheck find use-after-free?
  62  Yes in example 04 (cppcheck 2.13.0). It also reports a double free on line 12 that never happens when the code runs, so a
  63  finding needs checking too.
  64  
  65  ### Is running the code with AddressSanitizer enough?
  66  No. It only sees what your inputs reach. In example 05 the tests use normal input only: the line that causes the bug runs
  67  0 times, AddressSanitizer reports nothing, while gcc -fanalyzer and cppcheck find the bug.
  68  
  69  ### What is the difference between line coverage and testing the risky case?
  70  A line can run many times without the dangerous condition ever happening. In example 02, the buggy line runs 9 times on
  71  normal input; the bug only appears when the count equals the buffer size. This repo measures both with gcov.
  72  
  73  ### How should I report a static analysis or code review result?
  74  Report the CLEAN or BUG verdict together with the build settings, the kinds of input that were tried, how deep the testing
  75  went, and whether the test was shown able to fail. `STANDARD-v0.md` defines a short format for this, and
  76  `readout-template.json` is a fill-in version.
  77  
  78  ### Can I use this for AI code reviewers?
  79  Yes. An AI reviewer is just another checker: give it the same code, record its verdict per example and per run, and compare
  80  with running the code. Please share results with the "Checker result" issue template.
  81  
  82  ## Related work
  83  
  84  - **NIST SARD / Juliet test suite** (https://samate.nist.gov/SARD/): a large labelled corpus of synthetic C/C++ and Java
  85    test cases for scoring analyzers at scale. This repo is the opposite end: a few tiny cases you can read in a minute, plus
  86    a format for stating what a CLEAN result covers. The two are complementary.
  87  - **Static analyzer benchmark suites and comparison harnesses** run many tools over many cases and report scores. This repo
  88    does not rank tools; it shows, case by case, why a CLEAN verdict needs its build settings, input kinds and coverage
  89    depth stated next to it.
  90  
  91  ## Quick start (about 1 minute)
  92  
  93  With Docker (any OS):
  94  
  95  ```
  96  git clone https://github.com/ericyunlinchiang/certify-the-checker.git
  97  cd certify-the-checker
  98  docker build -t certify-the-checker . && docker run --rm certify-the-checker
  99  ```
 100  
 101  Without Docker: Linux with GNU **gcc 13+**, **clang**, **python3**; **cppcheck** optional.
 102  Ubuntu 24.04: `sudo apt-get install gcc clang cppcheck python3`. Ubuntu 22.04 ships an older gcc: use Docker. On macOS the
 103  `gcc` command is clang: use Docker.
 104  
 105  ```
 106  tools/run_all.sh                                   # the table above
 107  tools/run_example.sh examples/02-off-by-one        # one example in detail: lines, coverage, readout.json
 108  ```
 109  
 110  `tools/run_all.sh --check` compares your table with `examples/expected-results.txt`. A match means **you reproduced the
 111  same results**. It does not mean a checker is good. Other tool versions can give different results.
 112  
 113  ## How results are decided
 114  
 115  - Each example lists its **bug lines** in `example.env`: the root cause and the line where it goes wrong (for example
 116    01: line 17 computes the size in 16 bits, line 21 writes past the buffer).
 117  - A checker **finds the bug** if it reports any bug line. Other lines it reports are printed as notes.
 118  - Running the code: **BUG** if AddressSanitizer/UBSan reports an error in the example; **CLEAN** if it runs normally;
 119    **NOTRIGGER** if no bug line ran at all.
 120  - **Coverage depth** is measured with gcov for each kind of input: `none` (no bug line ran) < `partial` (some ran, often
 121    not the root cause) < `line` (all ran) < `branch` (and every branch in the function went both ways) < `input-class`
 122    (the input actually triggered the bug).
 123  - **Controlled** means at least one input makes the run report BUG. A run is only shown able to fail if that happens.
 124  
 125  Each run writes a `readout.json` that follows `schema/readout.schema.json` (checked in CI by `tools/validate_readout.py`).
 126  
 127  ## Use it on your own code (4 steps)
 128  
 129  1. **Pick a claim.** One place where your checker says CLEAN, or reports a finding.
 130  2. **Run it for real**, under a sanitizer or with tests, once per kind of input you care about (normal, empty, very
 131     large, negative, malformed...). Measure whether the risky line and branches actually ran (gcov or llvm-cov).
 132  3. **Show your test can fail**: use an input or a planted bug that must be reported.
 133  4. **Write it down** in the `readout-template.json` format, one cell per kind of input, and report the whole table.
 134  
 135  The scripts here are built for the curated examples, where the bug lines are known. On your own code you supply the kinds
 136  of input and decide which lines matter; to add an example to this repo, see `CONTRIBUTING.md`.
 137  
 138  ## Words used
 139  
 140  | Word | Meaning |
 141  |---|---|
 142  | CLEAN / BUG | "no issue found" / "issue found" |
 143  | checker (S) | the tool being evaluated: static analyzer, linter, AI reviewer |
 144  | running the code (X) | executing it and watching for errors, e.g. with AddressSanitizer |
 145  | certify-clean | checker says CLEAN and running the code found nothing, for the stated settings and inputs |
 146  | does not transfer | a CLEAN that holds for some settings or inputs but fails for others |
 147  | white-cell | a false negative: checker says CLEAN, running the code finds a real bug |
 148  | coverage depth | how thoroughly the risky code was exercised (see above) |
 149  | controlled | the test was shown able to fail |
 150  
 151  `STANDARD-v0.md` starts with a plain-language version, then the precise one.
 152

## FILE: STANDARD-v0.md

```
   1  # Certify-the-Checker — a Standard for Scoped Certification of a Checker's CLEAN Verdict (v0)
   2  
   3  ## Plain-language version (read this first)
   4  
   5  When a code checker says "no issues found" (CLEAN), that is a statement about what was checked, not about the code. This
   6  standard asks you to report a CLEAN result together with its scope:
   7  
   8  1. **What it was run on**: build settings and the kinds of input that were tried.
   9  2. **How deep the testing went**: did the risky line run at all; did every branch run; did the risky condition actually
  10     happen; was every kind of input tried.
  11  3. **Whether the test could have failed**: show it on a known bug first ("known-bug sanity check").
  12  
  13  Then compare the checker with actually running the code (for example under AddressSanitizer), one kind of input at a time,
  14  and report the whole table. Words used below, in plain terms:
  15  
  16  | Term in this document | Plain meaning |
  17  |---|---|
  18  | S, the checker | the static analyzer, linter or AI reviewer being evaluated |
  19  | X, execution oracle | running the code and watching for errors (sanitizers, tests) |
  20  | F, formal oracle | an optional proof or model-checking tool |
  21  | tau | the score cut-off a checker uses to say CLEAN or BUG |
  22  | certify-clean | checker says CLEAN, and running the code under the stated settings and inputs also found nothing |
  23  | non-transferability | a CLEAN that holds for some settings or inputs but fails for others |
  24  | white-cell | a false negative: checker says CLEAN, running the code finds a real bug |
  25  | corner | a known real bug (for example from a public advisory) that nothing in your setup observes |
  26  | coverage gap | the risky code never ran, so running the code says nothing about it |
  27  | positive control, CONTROLLED | a known-bug sanity check: the test was shown able to fail |
  28  | axiom accounting | list every assumption your result depends on |
  29  | cube-grade | a result produced under the full independence rules in section 7; anything else is advisory |
  30  
  31  The rest of this document is the precise version.
  32  
  33  ## Abstract
  34  Static analyzers and LLM-generated checkers emit CLEAN (no-finding) verdicts. A CLEAN verdict is easy to over-trust. This
  35  standard defines how to CERTIFY and, crucially, BOUND such a verdict by composing the checker with independent oracles and
  36  reporting a scoped disagreement/limitation map. It never issues a portable safety certificate. The core result it is built
  37  to express: **a clean verdict is scoped to the configuration and input class under which it was obtained, and does not
  38  transfer to another configuration or input class of the same unit.**
  39  
  40  ## 1. A composition contract
  41  What this standard defines is a stable CONTRACT that lets heterogeneous producers be composed into one coherent
  42  certification system, rather than any single oracle. The contract is the interface defined below: the verdict format, the
  43  join key, the coverage-depth levels, the positive-control grades, the independence protocol, and the axiom accounting. A
  44  static checker (S), a formal oracle (F), or an execution oracle (X) may be composed in, provided it honors the contract.
  45  The contract is domain-neutral: it applies to any checker on any target. A worked example is given in section 8.
  46  
  47  ## 2. Producers
  48  - S — the checker under certification (e.g. a static or LLM-generated checker). Emits a per-claim score; a threshold tau maps
  49    the score to BUG or CLEAN.
  50  - X — an execution oracle. Emits BUG, CLEAN, or NOTRIGGER, plus a coverage flag, a build configuration, and an oracle kind.
  51  - F — an optional formal oracle. Advisory unless it meets the cube-grade conditions (section 7).
  52  Each producer is scoped and run independently; no producer reads another producer's verdicts.
  53  
  54  ## 3. Core definitions
  55  - certify-clean(claim, tau): S=CLEAN AND X=CLEAN AND the claim's line was covered, under a STATED build configuration and
  56    input set, AND the property carries a positive control (section 4). It is nominal-run and coverage scoped. It is never a
  57    proof of absence and never a portable safety certificate. Every certify-clean states its coverage level (section 5), its
  58    configuration and input-class tag, and its control grade.
  59  - Non-transferability (the central law): a certify-clean obtained under configuration or input class C does not transfer to
  60    a configuration or input class C' of the same unit where a defect is observable. The mechanism is made precise by coverage
  61    depth (section 5): a line can execute many times while the defect's triggering condition or input class is never exercised.
  62  - white-cell(claim, tau): S=CLEAN AND X=BUG, line covered. A cell that a checker-trusting view does not predict.
  63  - corner(claim): a known-real defect (external ground truth, e.g. a public advisory) that no producer observes under the run
  64    configuration. Distinct from a coverage gap.
  65  - coverage-gap(claim): the line was not executed; the execution oracle is silent and says nothing about the claim.
  66  
  67  ## 4. Property positive control
  68  A property's CLEAN has a grade. CONTROLLED: the property's BUG path has been demonstrated on a planted positive (a mutant or
  69  a crafted input that must flip CLEAN to BUG). UNCONTROLLED otherwise. An uncontrolled CLEAN is a lower tier and may not alone
  70  support certify-clean. Report the grade per property.
  71  
  72  ## 5. Coverage depth
  73  "Covered" is stratified, weakest to strongest: LINE < BRANCH < CONDITION < INPUT-CLASS. Below LINE, a run may reach
  74  NONE or only PART of the relevant lines (for example the faulting line but not the root cause). A certify-clean states the level it
  75  reached. Line coverage (the defect line executed) is the floor and does not imply the defect's triggering condition or input
  76  class was ever exercised. This stratification is the precise account of why a clean verdict fails to transfer.
  77  
  78  ## 6. Reporting rules
  79  - R1 Report a trade-off curve over tau, never a single threshold.
  80  - R2 The deliverable is a scoped disagreement/limitation map, never a certified-safe claim.
  81  - R3 Every certify-clean carries its (configuration, input-class) tag; a claim stated without it is malformed.
  82  - R4 Coverage is reported explicitly (covered / total); thin cells are shown, not hidden behind an aggregate.
  83  - R5 X=BUG is trusted; X=CLEAN is coverage, not correctness; white-cells and corners are first-class, not footnotes.
  84  
  85  ## 7. Axiom accounting, independence, cube-grade
  86  - Axiom accounting: every result lists its declared axioms; a result that depends on an undeclared axiom is void. Declare the
  87    common target anchor, the S-threshold rule, that X=CLEAN is coverage not proof, the certify-clean definition, the
  88    white-cell/corner definitions, and any producer-specific transform (e.g. a source normalization, a host substitution).
  89  - Independence protocol: a shared target manifest (shared targets, never shared verdicts) issued before any matched run;
  90    any sealed property/configuration carries a publicly verifiable timestamp made before the checker is produced (a private
  91    timestamp is insufficient for a released claim); projecting one producer's frozen results onto another's positions is a
  92    projection, never a re-run informed by those positions; once any party has seen a producer's output or an external answer,
  93    it may not thereafter direct a different producer's scope, build, or configuration for the same target.
  94  - Cube-grade vs advisory: a verdict is cube-grade only if it answers a shared-manifest cell, was run independently, and
  95    declares its axioms; otherwise it is advisory and never gates. A thin or absent producer never downgrades a certify-clean;
  96    it only withholds corroboration.
  97  
  98  ## 8. Worked example (independently reproducible)
  99  This example ILLUSTRATES the definitions; it is not a cube-grade result (the independence protocol of section 7 is not
 100  exercised — it is the author's own code). It is tagged per R3: config host build, input-class {benign, adversarial},
 101  coverage depth line / input-class, execution positive-controlled by the adversarial input itself.
 102  ### 8.1 Integer truncation in a record parser (illustrative)
 103  A small record parser whose destination size is computed in a narrow integer type and truncates. Two REAL public static
 104  analyzers disagree on it: one (a clang static-analyzer run) is silent and returns CLEAN — a genuine under-approximation —
 105  while another (gcc's -fanalyzer) flags the write line as a heap buffer overflow. An execution oracle observes a heap
 106  out-of-bounds write under an adversarial input class, while the benign input class is clean. So the silent analyzer's CLEAN
 107  is scoped to the benign input class and does not transfer; and the two real checkers' disagreement is itself a cell on the
 108  map. (The author's own illustrative code; tool versions are pinned in the repository README; run it with
 109  tools/run_example.sh examples/01-integer-truncation. Further examples, including one where the checker finds a bug that the
 110  tests never reach, are in examples/.)
 111  
 112  ## 9. What this standard is not
 113  It does not certify safety. It does not rank tools. It does not claim a portable guarantee for any function. It reports where
 114  checkers and oracles are blind, with each claim tagged by the configuration, input class, coverage depth, and control grade
 115  under which it holds.
```

## FILE: examples/01-integer-truncation/example.env

```
   1  TITLE="Integer truncation: buffer size computed in 16 bits"
   2  FUNC=parse_record
   3  BUG_LINES="17 21"
   4  BUG_LINES_WHY="17 = 16-bit size computation (root cause); 21 = out-of-bounds write"
   5  CLASSES="normal large"
```

## FILE: examples/01-integer-truncation/target.c

```
   1  /* Illustrative target (author's own code; not a vulnerability report).
   2   * A record parser: [u16 count][count x u32 item]. The destination buffer size is computed
   3   * in a 16-bit type, so a large count TRUNCATES the size while the copy loop writes count*4 bytes.
   4   * Demonstrates: one real static analyzer (clang) stays silent (CLEAN) while another (gcc -fanalyzer)
   5   * flags it, and an execution oracle observes a heap out-of-bounds WRITE under an adversarial
   6   * input-class. The clean verdict is INPUT-CLASS-scoped and does not transfer. */
   7  #include <stdint.h>
   8  #include <stdlib.h>
   9  #include <string.h>
  10  
  11  /* returns 0 on success; the OOB (if any) happens inside, observable only by an execution oracle */
  12  int parse_record(const uint8_t *buf, size_t buf_len) {
  13      if (buf_len < 2) return -1;
  14      uint16_t n;
  15      memcpy(&n, buf, 2);
  16      if ((size_t)2 + (size_t)n * 4u > buf_len) return -1;   /* SOURCE-read bound: fully guarded */
  17      uint16_t sz = (uint16_t)(n * 4);                        /* DEST size in 16-bit -> truncates */
  18      uint8_t *out = (uint8_t *)malloc(sz ? sz : 1);
  19      if (!out) return -1;
  20      for (uint16_t i = 0; i < n; i++) {
  21          memcpy(out + (size_t)i * 4, buf + 2 + (size_t)i * 4, 4); /* writes n*4 into sz-sized out */
  22      }
  23      free(out);
  24      return 0;
  25  }
```

## FILE: examples/01-integer-truncation/harness.c

```
   1  /* Drives parse_record with one input class per run: ./x normal | ./x large */
   2  #include <stdio.h>
   3  #include <stdint.h>
   4  #include <stdlib.h>
   5  #include <string.h>
   6  int parse_record(const uint8_t *buf, size_t buf_len);
   7  static uint8_t *mk(uint16_t n, size_t *len) { *len = 2 + (size_t)n * 4; uint8_t *b = malloc(*len); memcpy(b, &n, 2);
   8    for (size_t i = 2; i < *len; i++) b[i] = (uint8_t)i; return b; }
   9  int main(int argc, char **argv) {
  10    uint16_t n = (argc > 1 && strcmp(argv[1], "large") == 0) ? 16384 : 4;  /* 16384*4 = 65536 wraps a 16-bit size */
  11    size_t L; uint8_t *b = mk(n, &L); int rc = parse_record(b, L); free(b); printf("rc=%d\n", rc); return 0;
  12  }
```

## FILE: examples/02-off-by-one/target.c

```
   1  /* Off-by-one: the guard allows n == CAP, but the loop runs n+1 times. */
   2  #include <stdint.h>
   3  #include <string.h>
   4  #define CAP 16
   5  int copy_items(const uint8_t *buf, size_t len) {
   6      uint8_t dst[CAP];
   7      if (len < 1) return -1;
   8      size_t n = buf[0];
   9      if (n > CAP || len < 1 + n) return -1;
  10      for (size_t i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
  11          dst[i] = buf[1 + (i < n ? i : 0)];
  12      }
  13      return dst[0];
  14  }
```

## FILE: examples/03-signed-length/target.c

```
   1  /* Signed length: a negative length passes the "too big" check and is then used as a size. */
   2  #include <stdint.h>
   3  #include <stdlib.h>
   4  #include <string.h>
   5  #define MAX 64
   6  int read_field(const uint8_t *buf, size_t len, uint8_t *out) {
   7      if (len < 4) return -1;
   8      int32_t n;
   9      memcpy(&n, buf, 4);
  10      if (n > MAX) return -1;
  11      if ((size_t)4 + (size_t)(uint32_t)n > len && n >= 0) return -1;
  12      memcpy(out, buf + 4, (size_t)n);
  13      return n;
  14  }
```

## FILE: examples/04-use-after-free/target.c

```
   1  /* Use after free on an error path that only runs for one kind of input. */
   2  #include <stdint.h>
   3  #include <stdlib.h>
   4  #include <string.h>
   5  int handle(const uint8_t *buf, size_t len) {
   6      uint8_t *p = calloc(32, 1);
   7      if (!p) return -1;
   8      int bad = 0;
   9      if (len > 0 && buf[0] == 0xFF) { free(p); bad = 1; }
  10      int v = 0;
  11      if (len > 1 && buf[1] == 0xEE) v = p[0];
  12      if (!bad) free(p);
  13      return v + bad;
  14  }
```

```
   1  /* Not a memory bug: the average of an empty list divides by zero. */
   2  #include <stddef.h>
   3  int average(const int *v, size_t n) {
   4      long sum = 0;
   5      for (size_t i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += v[i];
   6      return (int)(sum / (long)n);
   7  }

## FILE: tools/run_all.sh

```
   1  #!/usr/bin/env bash
   2  # Run every example and print the results table.
   3  # Usage: tools/run_all.sh [--check]
   4  #   --check  compares the results with examples/expected-results.txt and fails on any difference.
   5  #            It checks that you get the SAME results as the README (reproducibility), not that a checker is good.
   6  # Set CTC_OUT=<dir> to keep all raw outputs and readout.json files (CI does this and publishes them).
   7  set -uo pipefail
   8  ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
   9  need() { command -v "$1" >/dev/null 2>&1 || { echo "MISSING TOOL: $1 (see README: Requirements, or use the Dockerfile)"; exit 2; }; }
  10  need gcc; need clang; need gcov; need python3
  11  if gcc --version 2>/dev/null | head -1 | grep -qi clang; then
  12    echo "Your 'gcc' is really clang (common on macOS). Use the Dockerfile (see README)."; exit 2; fi
  13  gmaj=$(gcc -dumpversion | cut -d. -f1)
  14  [ "$gmaj" -ge 13 ] 2>/dev/null || { echo "gcc $gmaj found; gcc >= 13 is needed. Use the Dockerfile (see README)."; exit 2; }
  15  command -v cppcheck >/dev/null 2>&1 || echo "(cppcheck not installed: its column shows SKIPPED and --check will report a difference)"
  16  res="$(mktemp)"; trap 'rm -f "$res"' EXIT
  17  for d in "$ROOT"/examples/*/; do "$ROOT/tools/run_example.sh" "$d" --quiet | grep '^RESULT' >> "$res"; done
  18  echo
  19  echo "| example | clang --analyze | gcc -fanalyzer | cppcheck | running the code (per kind of input) |"
  20  echo "|---|---|---|---|---|"
  21  while read -r _ name c g p rest; do
  22    echo "| $name | ${c#clang=} | ${g#gcc=} | ${p#cppcheck=} | ${rest#exec: } |"
  23  done < "$res"
  24  if [ -n "${CTC_OUT:-}" ]; then
  25    python3 - "$CTC_OUT" <<'PY'
  26  import json, glob, os, sys
  27  out = sys.argv[1]
  28  docs = [json.load(open(f)) for f in sorted(glob.glob(os.path.join(out, '*', 'readout.json')))]
  29  json.dump({'standard': 'certify-the-checker v0', 'readouts': docs}, open(os.path.join(out, 'results.json'), 'w'), indent=2)
  30  print('\nall readouts: %s' % os.path.join(out, 'results.json'))
  31  PY
  32  fi
  33  if [ "${1:-}" = "--check" ]; then
  34    if diff <(sed 's/^RESULT //' "$res") "$ROOT/examples/expected-results.txt" >/dev/null; then
  35      echo; echo "CHECK: same results as examples/expected-results.txt (reproduced)"
  36    else echo; echo "CHECK: results DIFFER from examples/expected-results.txt (other tool versions?)"
  37      diff <(sed 's/^RESULT //' "$res") "$ROOT/examples/expected-results.txt"; exit 1; fi
  38  fi
```

## FILE: tools/run_example.sh

```
   1  #!/usr/bin/env bash
   2  # Run one example:
   3  #   1. three static checkers on target.c (raw output kept),
   4  #   2. the code itself under AddressSanitizer + UBSan, one run per input class,
   5  #   3. a coverage build (gcov) per input class, to measure how deep each run went.
   6  # Then tools/readout.py prints a summary and writes readout.json (schema: schema/readout.schema.json).
   7  # Usage: tools/run_example.sh examples/<name> [--quiet]
   8  # Raw outputs go to $CTC_OUT/<name>/ if CTC_OUT is set, otherwise to a temporary directory.
   9  set -uo pipefail
  10  ROOT="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/.." && pwd)"
  11  DIR="$(cd "${1:?usage: tools/run_example.sh examples/<name>}" && pwd)"
  12  QUIET="${2:-}"
  13  NAME="$(basename "$DIR")"
  14  # shellcheck disable=SC1091
  15  source "$DIR/example.env"   # TITLE FUNC BUG_LINES BUG_LINES_WHY CLASSES
  16  if [ -n "${CTC_OUT:-}" ]; then mkdir -p "$CTC_OUT"; OUT="$(cd "$CTC_OUT" && pwd)/$NAME"; rm -rf "$OUT"; mkdir -p "$OUT"; KEEP=1
  17  else OUT="$(mktemp -d)"; KEEP=0; fi
  18  mkdir -p "$OUT/static" "$OUT/exec" "$OUT/cov"
  19  WORK="$(mktemp -d)"; trap 'rm -rf "$WORK"; [ "$KEEP" = 1 ] || rm -rf "$OUT"' EXIT
  20  
  21  # 1. static checkers (run from the example dir so reported paths are "target.c:LINE")
  22  (cd "$DIR" && clang --analyze -o /dev/null target.c) > "$OUT/static/clang.txt" 2>&1
  23  (cd "$DIR" && gcc -Wall -Wextra -fanalyzer -c target.c -o /dev/null) > "$OUT/static/gcc.txt" 2>&1
  24  if command -v cppcheck >/dev/null 2>&1; then
  25    (cd "$DIR" && cppcheck --enable=all --suppress=missingIncludeSystem --suppress=unusedFunction --quiet target.c) \
  26      > "$OUT/static/cppcheck.txt" 2>&1
  27  else echo "SKIPPED: cppcheck not installed" > "$OUT/static/cppcheck.skipped"; fi
  28  
  29  # 2. execution under ASan + UBSan, one process per input class
  30  gcc -std=c11 -g -O0 -fsanitize=address,undefined -fno-sanitize-recover=all \
  31      "$DIR/harness.c" "$DIR/target.c" -o "$WORK/x_san" 2>"$OUT/exec/build.log" \
  32    || { echo "BUILD FAILED (sanitizer build)"; cat "$OUT/exec/build.log"; exit 3; }
  33  for c in $CLASSES; do "$WORK/x_san" "$c" > "$OUT/exec/$c.txt" 2>&1; echo $? > "$OUT/exec/$c.rc"; done
  34  
  35  # 3. coverage build (no sanitizers), one run per input class, gcov JSON with branch data
  36  cp "$DIR/target.c" "$DIR/harness.c" "$WORK/"
  37  ( cd "$WORK" && gcc -std=c11 -g -O0 --coverage -fno-stack-protector \
  38      harness.c target.c "$ROOT/tools/support/gcov_dump_on_crash.c" -o x_cov ) 2>"$OUT/cov/build.log" \
  39    || { echo "BUILD FAILED (coverage build)"; cat "$OUT/cov/build.log"; exit 3; }
  40  for c in $CLASSES; do
  41    ( cd "$WORK" && rm -f ./*.gcda && { ./x_cov "$c" >/dev/null 2>&1 || true; }
  42      gcov -b --json-format --stdout x_cov-target.gcda > "$OUT/cov/$c.json" 2>/dev/null ) 2>/dev/null
  43  done
  44  
  45  echo "gcc $(gcc -dumpfullversion), clang $(clang --version | sed -n '1s/.*version \([0-9.]*\).*/\1/p'), cppcheck $(cppcheck --version 2>/dev/null | awk '{print $2}'), gcov $(gcov --version | head -1 | awk '{print $NF}')" > "$OUT/versions.txt"
  46  python3 "$ROOT/tools/readout.py" "$DIR" "$OUT" ${QUIET:+--quiet}
```

## FILE: tools/readout.py

```
   1  #!/usr/bin/env python3
   2  """Turn the raw outputs of tools/run_example.sh into a summary and a readout.json.
   3  
   4  Rules (also written in README.md):
   5  - A static checker "finds the bug" if it reports any line listed in BUG_LINES.
   6  - Execution: BUG if AddressSanitizer/UBSan reports an error in target.c for that input class; CLEAN if the run
   7    exits normally; NOTRIGGER if no bug line was executed (the run says nothing about the bug).
   8  - Coverage depth per input class, measured with gcov:
   9      input-class  the run triggered the bug (the risky condition was exercised);
  10      branch       every bug line ran and every branch in the function was taken both ways;
  11      line         every bug line ran, but some branch in the function was not taken both ways;
  12      partial      some bug lines ran, others (often the root cause) never ran;
  13      none         no bug line ran.
  14    For an input class that triggers the bug, the coverage numbers are not reported: the coverage build has no
  15    sanitizer, so the bug itself can corrupt the run.
  16  - Control grade: "controlled" if at least one input class makes execution report BUG (the check is shown able to
  17    fail on this target); otherwise "uncontrolled".
  18  """
  19  import json, os, re, shlex, sys
  20  
  21  def load_env(path):
  22      env = {}
  23      for line in open(path):
  24          line = line.strip()
  25          if not line or line.startswith('#') or '=' not in line:
  26              continue
  27          k, v = line.split('=', 1)
  28          env[k] = ' '.join(shlex.split(v))
  29      return env
  30  
  31  def reported_lines(text):
  32      return sorted({int(m) for m in re.findall(r'target\.c:(\d+)', text)})
  33  
  34  def main():
  35      d, out = sys.argv[1], sys.argv[2]
  36      quiet = '--quiet' in sys.argv[3:]
  37      env = load_env(os.path.join(d, 'example.env'))
  38      name = os.path.basename(os.path.normpath(d))
  39      bug = [int(x) for x in env['BUG_LINES'].split()]
  40      classes = env['CLASSES'].split()
  41  
  42      # static checkers
  43      checkers = {}
  44      for key, label in (('clang', 'clang --analyze'), ('gcc', 'gcc -Wall -Wextra -fanalyzer'),
  45                         ('cppcheck', 'cppcheck --enable=all')):
  46          p = os.path.join(out, 'static', key + '.txt')
  47          if not os.path.exists(p):
  48              checkers[key] = {'label': label, 'verdict': 'SKIPPED', 'lines': []}
  49              continue
  50          lines = reported_lines(open(p, errors='replace').read())
  51          checkers[key] = {'label': label, 'lines': lines,
  52                           'verdict': 'BUG' if any(l in bug for l in lines) else 'CLEAN'}
  53  
  54      # coverage per class
  55      cov = {}
  56      for c in classes:
  57          info = {'bug_lines_run': {}, 'branches_total': 0, 'branches_taken': 0, 'untaken_branch_lines': []}
  58          p = os.path.join(out, 'cov', c + '.json')
  59          try:
  60              doc = json.loads(open(p).read().strip().splitlines()[0])
  61              for f in doc['files']:
  62                  if not f['file'].endswith('target.c'):
  63                      continue
  64                  for ln in f['lines']:
  65                      n = ln['line_number']
  66                      if n in bug:
  67                          info['bug_lines_run'][n] = ln['count']
  68                      for b in ln.get('branches', []):
  69                          info['branches_total'] += 1
  70                          if b['count'] > 0:
  71                              info['branches_taken'] += 1
  72                          elif n not in info['untaken_branch_lines']:
  73                              info['untaken_branch_lines'].append(n)
  74          except (OSError, ValueError, IndexError, KeyError):
  75              info['error'] = 'no coverage data'
  76          for n in bug:
  77              info['bug_lines_run'].setdefault(n, 0)
  78          cov[c] = info
  79  
  80      # execution per class
  81      exe = {}
  82      for c in classes:
  83          text = open(os.path.join(out, 'exec', c + '.txt'), errors='replace').read()
  84          rc = int(open(os.path.join(out, 'exec', c + '.rc')).read().strip() or '0')
  85          san = ('ERROR: AddressSanitizer' in text or 'runtime error:' in text) and 'target.c:' in text
  86          any_bug_line_ran = any(v > 0 for v in cov[c]['bug_lines_run'].values())
  87          if san:
  88              m = re.search(r'target\.c:(\d+)', text)
  89              exe[c] = {'verdict': 'BUG', 'line': int(m.group(1)) if m else None}
  90          elif not any_bug_line_ran:
  91              exe[c] = {'verdict': 'NOTRIGGER', 'line': None}
  92          elif rc == 0:
  93              exe[c] = {'verdict': 'CLEAN', 'line': None}
  94          else:
  95              exe[c] = {'verdict': 'ERROR', 'line': None, 'rc': rc}
  96  
  97      def depth(c):
  98          if exe[c]['verdict'] == 'BUG':
  99              return 'input-class'
 100          runs = cov[c]['bug_lines_run']
 101          if not runs or max(runs.values()) == 0:
 102              return 'none'
 103          if min(runs.values()) == 0:
 104              return 'partial'
 105          if cov[c]['branches_total'] and cov[c]['branches_taken'] == cov[c]['branches_total']:
 106              return 'branch'
 107          return 'line'
 108  
 109      controlled = any(e['verdict'] == 'BUG' for e in exe.values())
 110  
 111      def result(cv, ev, dep):
 112          if ev == 'NOTRIGGER':
 113              return 'not covered'
 114          if cv == 'SKIPPED':
 115              return 'checker not run'
 116          if cv == 'CLEAN' and ev == 'BUG':
 117              return 'checker missed a real bug'
 118          if cv == 'BUG' and ev == 'BUG':
 119              return 'both found it'
 120          if cv == 'BUG' and ev == 'CLEAN':
 121              return 'checker reports a bug that this input did not trigger'
 122          if cv == 'CLEAN' and ev == 'CLEAN':
 123              return 'certify_clean' if controlled else 'clean, but uncontrolled'
 124          return 'error'
 125  
 126      cells = []
 127      for key, ch in checkers.items():
 128          for c in classes:
 129              dep = depth(c)
 130              cells.append({'input_class': c, 'checker': ch['label'], 'checker_verdict': ch['verdict'],
 131                            'execution': exe[c]['verdict'], 'coverage_depth': dep,
 132                            'result': result(ch['verdict'], exe[c]['verdict'], dep)})
 133  
 134      readout = {
 135          'standard': 'certify-the-checker v0',
 136          'claim_id': name,
 137          'location': 'examples/%s/target.c lines %s' % (name, ' '.join(map(str, bug))),
 138          'bug_lines_why': env.get('BUG_LINES_WHY', ''),
 139          'build_config': 'host build: ' + open(os.path.join(out, 'versions.txt')).read().strip()
 140                          if os.path.exists(os.path.join(out, 'versions.txt')) else 'host build',
 141          'checkers': {ch['label']: ch['verdict'] for ch in checkers.values()},
 142          'cells': cells,
 143          'coverage': {c: ({'note': 'the run hit the bug; coverage not reported'} if exe[c]['verdict'] == 'BUG' else
 144                           {'bug_lines_run': {str(k): v for k, v in cov[c]['bug_lines_run'].items()},
 145                            'branches_taken': cov[c]['branches_taken'], 'branches_total': cov[c]['branches_total']})
 146                       for c in classes},
 147          'control_grade': 'controlled' if controlled else 'uncontrolled',
 148          'note': "Illustration with the author's own code; not a vulnerability report.",
 149      }
 150      with open(os.path.join(out, 'readout.json'), 'w') as f:
 151          json.dump(readout, f, indent=2)
 152  
 153      if not quiet:
 154          print('== %s: %s' % (name, env['TITLE']))
 155          print('   bug lines: %s  (%s)' % (' '.join(map(str, bug)), env.get('BUG_LINES_WHY', '')))
 156          print('   %-30s %-8s %s' % ('static checker', 'verdict', 'lines it reported'))
 157          for ch in checkers.values():
 158              print('   %-30s %-8s %s' % (ch['label'], ch['verdict'], ' '.join(map(str, ch['lines'])) or '-'))
 159          print('   running the code (ASan + UBSan), one run per input class, with measured coverage:')
 160          for c in classes:
 161              e, v = exe[c], cov[c]
 162              if e['verdict'] == 'BUG':
 163                  detail = 'the run hit the bug'
 164              else:
 165                  detail = ', '.join('line %d ran %dx' % (k, n) for k, n in sorted(v['bug_lines_run'].items()))
 166                  detail += '; branches taken %d/%d' % (v['branches_taken'], v['branches_total'])
 167              print('     %-12s %-9s depth=%-11s %s' % (
 168                  c, e['verdict'] + (' @%d' % e['line'] if e.get('line') else ''), depth(c), detail))
 169          print('   control grade: %s' % readout['control_grade'])
 170          for ch in checkers.values():
 171              for n in ch['lines']:
 172                  if n not in bug:
 173                      print('   note: %s also reported line %d; it is not a bug line, and no run confirmed a bug there.'
 174                            % (ch['label'], n))
 175          print('   readout written: %s' % os.path.join(out, 'readout.json'))
 176      print('RESULT %s clang=%s gcc=%s cppcheck=%s exec:%s' % (
 177          name, checkers['clang']['verdict'], checkers['gcc']['verdict'], checkers['cppcheck']['verdict'],
 178          ''.join(' %s=%s' % (c, exe[c]['verdict']) for c in classes)))
 179  
 180  if __name__ == '__main__':
 181      main()
```

## FILE: tools/validate_readout.py

```
   1  #!/usr/bin/env python3
   2  """Check readout.json files against schema/readout.schema.json (required keys and allowed values only; stdlib, no
   3  dependencies). Usage: tools/validate_readout.py FILE [FILE...]"""
   4  import json, os, sys
   5  
   6  def check(obj, sch, path, errs):
   7      if 'enum' in sch and obj not in sch['enum']:
   8          errs.append('%s: %r not in %s' % (path, obj, sch['enum']))
   9      t = sch.get('type')
  10      if t == 'object':
  11          if not isinstance(obj, dict):
  12              errs.append('%s: not an object' % path); return
  13          for k in sch.get('required', []):
  14              if k not in obj:
  15                  errs.append('%s: missing %s' % (path, k))
  16          for k, v in obj.items():
  17              if k in sch.get('properties', {}):
  18                  check(v, sch['properties'][k], path + '.' + k, errs)
  19              elif isinstance(sch.get('additionalProperties'), dict):
  20                  check(v, sch['additionalProperties'], path + '.' + k, errs)
  21      elif t == 'array':
  22          if not isinstance(obj, list):
  23              errs.append('%s: not a list' % path); return
  24          if len(obj) < sch.get('minItems', 0):
  25              errs.append('%s: too few items' % path)
  26          for i, v in enumerate(obj):
  27              check(v, sch.get('items', {}), '%s[%d]' % (path, i), errs)
  28      elif t == 'string' and not isinstance(obj, str):
  29          errs.append('%s: not a string' % path)
  30  
  31  schema = json.load(open(os.path.join(os.path.dirname(__file__), '..', 'schema', 'readout.schema.json')))
  32  bad = 0
  33  for f in sys.argv[1:]:
  34      errs = []
  35      check(json.load(open(f)), schema, '$', errs)
  36      print(('OK   ' if not errs else 'FAIL ') + f)
  37      for e in errs:
  38          print('     ' + e)
  39      bad += bool(errs)
  40  sys.exit(1 if bad else 0)
```

## FILE: tools/support/gcov_dump_on_crash.c

```
   1  /* Linked only into the coverage build: write coverage data even if the program crashes. */
   2  #include <signal.h>
   3  #include <unistd.h>
   4  extern void __gcov_dump(void);
   5  static void on_crash(int sig) { __gcov_dump(); _exit(128 + sig); }
   6  __attribute__((constructor)) static void install(void) {
   7    signal(SIGSEGV, on_crash); signal(SIGABRT, on_crash); signal(SIGBUS, on_crash); signal(SIGFPE, on_crash);
   8  }
```

## FILE: Dockerfile

```
   1  # Same tools as the results table: Ubuntu 24.04, gcc 13, clang 18, cppcheck 2.13.
   2  # Build:  docker build -t certify-the-checker .
   3  # Run:    docker run --rm certify-the-checker            (prints the table and checks it)
   4  FROM ubuntu:24.04
   5  RUN apt-get update \
   6   && apt-get install -y --no-install-recommends gcc clang cppcheck python3 bash ca-certificates \
   7   && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*
   8  WORKDIR /work
   9  COPY . /work
  10  CMD ["tools/run_all.sh", "--check"]
```

   1  name: examples
   2  on:
   3    push:
   4    pull_request:
   5    workflow_dispatch:

   7    contents: read
   8  jobs:

  14          run: sudo apt-get update && sudo apt-get install -y gcc clang cppcheck python3
  15        - name: Tool versions
  16          run: gcc --version | head -1; clang --version | head -1; cppcheck --version; gcov --version | head -1
  17        - name: Check file hashes
  18          run: sha256sum -c SHA256SUMS
  19        - name: Check that DIGEST.md is up to date
  20          run: tools/make_digest.sh > /tmp/DIGEST.md && diff -u DIGEST.md /tmp/DIGEST.md
  21        - name: Run all examples and compare with expected results
  22          run: CTC_OUT=results tools/run_all.sh --check
  23        - name: Validate every readout against the schema

  25        - name: Publish raw outputs (checker output, sanitizer output, coverage, readouts)
  26          if: always()

  28          with:

  30            path: results/
  31    docker:

## FILE: CONTRIBUTING.md

```
   1  # Contributing
   2  
   3  Contributions of all sizes are welcome. You do not need a security background.
   4  
   5  ## 1. Share a checker result (easiest)
   6  Run any checker you have (Coverity, CodeQL, Semgrep, Infer, PVS-Studio, Clang-Tidy, an AI code reviewer, ...) on
   7  `examples/*/target.c` and open an issue with the **Checker result** template. Include the checker version and the exact
   8  command, so others can reproduce it. Results that disagree with the table are the most interesting ones.
   9  
  10  ## 2. Add an example
  11  Each example is one folder in `examples/` with three small files:
  12  
  13  - `target.c`: one function with one bug, written by you for this repository (no third-party code, no real vulnerabilities
  14    in other projects);
  15  - `harness.c`: a `main` that takes the input-class name as its first argument and calls the function once;
  16  - `example.env`: `TITLE`, `FUNC` (function name), `BUG_LINES` (root-cause line and the line where it goes wrong),
  17    `BUG_LINES_WHY` (one sentence per line), `CLASSES` (kinds of input; usually at least one fine and one that triggers the bug).
  18  
  19  Then:
  20  
  21  1. run `tools/run_example.sh examples/<your-folder>` and check the output looks right;
  22  2. run `tools/run_all.sh`, then update `examples/expected-results.txt` with the new line;
  23  3. regenerate `DIGEST.md` (`tools/make_digest.sh > DIGEST.md`) and `SHA256SUMS`:
  24     `find . -type f ! -name SHA256SUMS ! -path './.git/*' | sed 's|^\./||' | LC_ALL=C sort | xargs sha256sum > SHA256SUMS`;
  25  4. open a pull request. CI runs every example on Ubuntu 24.04, checks the table, validates the readouts and publishes raw outputs.
  26  
  27  Good examples are short (under 30 lines) and have one clear bug. Cases where a checker says CLEAN are welcome, and so are
  28  cases where a checker finds what the tests miss: the point is an honest table, not a one-sided one.
  29  
  30  ## 3. Improve the standard
  31  Open an issue or pull request against `STANDARD-v0.md`. Explain the problem with a concrete case if you can.
  32  
  33  ## License of contributions
  34  By contributing you agree that text is licensed CC BY 4.0 and code Apache-2.0, as for the rest of the repository.
```

## FILE: PROVENANCE.md

```
   1  # Provenance
   2  
   3  - Standard (STANDARD-v0.md): written by the author. Its building blocks are common public engineering ideas: static and
   4    LLM-generated checkers under-approximate; execution and formal oracles have different blind spots; a clean verdict holds
   5    only for the configuration and inputs it was obtained under; coverage has depth (line / branch / condition / input class).
   6  - Examples: targets, harnesses and scripts are the author's own code, written for this repository. The checkers are three
   7    public static analyzers run unmodified (clang's static analyzer, gcc -fanalyzer, cppcheck); execution uses
   8    AddressSanitizer and UBSan; coverage is measured with gcov. Tool versions are listed in the README.
   9  - These files were prepared and reproduced in a personal environment, using only public tools.
```
